text: Plato's two laws concerning the gods (Republic 379a–383c) make Genesis 6 a difficult chapter to read alongside the Republic. In Genesis "it grieved him at his heart" (6:6), and Yahweh resolves to destroy every living thing (6:7). By Plato's standards he is both moved and a cause of harm. Plato framed his laws against gods who do evil from caprice, however, and the flood has a reason: "the earth was filled with violence" (6:11). That reason narrows the conflict with the Republic without removing it. Plato allows a god to punish if the poet can show that the punishment is just and that the one punished is made better by it (380a–b). No one is made better by a flood. Grief he does not allow at all, because to be grieved is to be changed. For Plato a good god cannot be affected by what lies below him. For Genesis a good God is affected by what his creatures have become, and his grief shows how seriously he takes their corruption. Noah and Socrates also arrive at theology at different points in their building. Noah builds under judgment from the beginning, to dimensions given by God (6:15), and that God has looked at the world and been wounded by it. Socrates derives his city from human need (369b–c) and reaches theology only when the guardians must be educated. Both texts read inner disorder on a larger scale. Genesis moves from "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart" (6:5) to an earth filled with violence. Socrates looks for justice written larger in a city (368d). When the readings break off, both constructions are unfinished: the ark waits for its passengers, and the city waits for its rulers.
